newsitem.title: FRANCE: Zaire talks highlight French loss of Africa power.
newsitem.headline: Zaire talks highlight French loss of Africa power.

text.p: While ailing Zaire President Mobutu Sese Seko and triumphant rebel leader Laurent Kabila held peace talks aboard a South African navy ship off Congo's coastline, the French ambassador waited impotently ashore for news.

The exclusion of Paris's man in Brazzaville from Sunday's U.S.-brokered meeting, chaired by South African President Nelson Mandela, highlighted France's sharp loss of influence on a continent it long regarded as its backyard.

Stephen Smith, Africa expert of the Paris daily Liberation, noted that Mobutu, one of Africa's longest-serving French-backed strongmen, had chosen to announce his agreement to resign in a letter to U.S. President Bill Clinton. The French authorities only found out about it by reading the New York Times, he said.

"Yesterday, for the first time in 40 years, France was absent from a negotiation on the future of Africa when it should have been the organiser," political commentator Michele Cotta said on RTL radio.
"France is isolated and abandoned, consecrating the rise of American domination in Africa," she said.
Referring to a longtime French kingmaker, who died recently after decades of making and breaking African leaders, Cotta said: "Jacques Foccart died a second death yesterday."

Two close French allies -- Presidents Pascal Lissouba of Congo and Gnassingbe Eyadema of Togo -- were also prevented from boarding the SAS Outeniqua, a customised icebreaker, compounding France's exclusion from the diplomatic ice-breaking.

Diplomats said France's isolation was a logical consequence of its stubborn support for Mobutu, who has long been ostracised by the international community for his government's record on corruption and human rights.
A few weeks ago, French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette was still calling Mobutu the "indispensible man".

Now the cancer-ridden ruler, once branded "a walking safe in a leopard-skin hat" by a more critical French minister, appears to face the choice between leaving voluntarily or being chased out of his capital, Kinshasa, by the advancing rebels.
French policy has seemed hopelessly overtaken by events.

When Kabila's forces began capturing a swathe of territory in eastern Zaire last October, Paris reacted by pleading for international military intervention to protect refugees displaced by the conflict.
The United States prevented such action even after the U.N. Security Council had approved a humanitarian operation.
Government spokesmen tried to play down France's humiliation, which raises questions about its ability to retain the allegiance of other longtime allies such as oil-rich Gabon's President Omar Bongo.

French Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt said Sunday's summit at sea "shows that the efforts of South Africa, the United Nations, the United States and France are starting to bear fruit".
Asked about the exclusion of French ambassador Raymond Cesaire from the Outeniqua, Rummehardt said U.S. envoy Bill Richardson had not been on the ship during the talks either.

He did not need to be. It was Washington's man who delivered both Kabila and Mobutu to the table, and who was at rebel headquarters in Lubumbashi on Monday trying to persuade Kabila to avoid a bloodbath in Kinshasa and allow an orderly transfer of power by giving Mobutu time to go quietly.
"Despite the official denials on both sides, how can it be doubted that France and the United States have waged a war of succession in Zaire?" Smith wrote.

France's loss of sway in the former Belgian colony was only the latest in a series of reverses that began with a 50 percent devaluation of the CFA franc linking 14 West African states with the French currency in 1994.
The ousting of a French-backed Hutu-dominated government by Ugandan-backed Tutsi rebels in Rwanda the same year was a precursor to the fall of Zaire.

France's image on the continent, devalued by the devaluation and tarnished by massacres committed by Hutu extremists, was also hurt by images of the ejection by riot police of African immigrants fighting deportation from a Paris church last year.

French President Jacques Chirac declares himself an "Afro-optimist" and has frequently used the international stage to call for increased development aid. But his government shows little sign of drawing on the lessons of its debacle in Zaire to forge a coherent new Africa policy.
